comments.author: @stanleybarton
comments.text: I just watched your production about what was East Germany. I enjoyed your objective and honest reporting. I look forward to learning more about the world from your perspective.  We Americans are woefully ignorant of modern European history. We need the kind of information provided by your programs.

comments.author: @leechumbley5440
comments.text: What a captivating introduction. I had no idea when and how Lascaux was discovered. Thank you for the story of the 4 boys. Many thanks also for reminding the listener of the cruel merciless Albigensian Crusade against the Cathars, which was all about Valois and Papal power. The Cité de Carcasonne, so popular today with tourists, was massively fortified to assert the power of the foreign French king in Paris, after he forcibly annexed the Midi (the Valois territory had previously extended no further south than the Loire). The Occitan language was suppressed, Gascon forbidden in 1463 ,and in 1539 the Villers Cotterêts' Edict allowed only French in official acts. In the 19th century there was a project for the elimination  throughout France of Occitan, Catalan, Basque, Breton, and several other ancient languages. School pupils in the Midi were punished  for speaking Occitan on school premises - 'la vergonha' (‘the shame‘). In Brittany pupils caught speaking Breton had to wear ‘le symbole.‘ How important that the 1904 Nobel Prize in Literature went to Fréderic Mistral for his works in Occitan. Alsace’s changing hands 4 times in short succession deserves one’s attention. The poignant book Marthe et Mathilde treats this subject sensitively  . Marthe Réling and Mathilde Goerke—two friends from Alsace—lived through a turbulent era in a region torn by war between France and Germany. Their story mirrors the history of Alsace itself, spanning the years from their birth in 1902 to their deaths in 2001. Like their fellow Alsatians, they grappled painfully with issues of identity and migration, as well as the unexpected turn of history that followed the Second World War.  I adore Paris, but let us not allow the City of Love blur out all the other wonderful places in France.

replies.author: @WhereonEarth4K
replies.text: That's exactly why we wanted the four boys and Lascaux to open the story — before it becomes about crusades and forced silence, it starts with wonder. The Occitan and Alsace threads you laid out deserve far more attention than they usually get. Appreciate you giving them the space here.
